At approximately 1.5ps, we observe the formation of an EZEE intermediate that arises due to rotation of  in the EEEE intermediate. An alternate pathway to form EZEE was observed via A'', where rotation around  was followed by isomerization around the C -C bond ( in Figure 2). Our previous simulations 2 3 revealed 22% of the wavepacket followed an alternate nonradiative relaxation pathway involving the isomerization around , resulting in approximately 4% EEZE intermediate. At 2ps, we observe the formation of a relatively long-lived EZZE intermediate resulting from rotation around the C - 5 C bond ( in Figure 2) Additionally, we showed the majority of the wavepacket (~64%) returns 6 back to the photoreactant forming “hot” EEZZ. Being sufficiently “hot,” approximately 7% of the wavepacket continues on to isomerize around  forming an  intermediate that has been observed by Feringa and coworkers.25 On a later timescale, we observe the formation of a ZEZZ intermediate as a result of rotation around  which also has been hypothesized via static calculations but, until now, has yet to be confirmed25 9 LLNL-JRNL-822958 In conclusion, we have shown for the first time the complete photoswitching mechanism for Meldrum’s Acid 1st generation DASAs using a discovery-based computational approach based on ab initio molecular dynamics. Our ~2ns of AIMS/AIMD goes well beyond identifying the few intermediates measured via time-resolved spectroscopy (A', B'', B''', and EZZZ) and unravels a rich chemistry consisting of several species and pathways (A', A'', B/B', B'', B''', EEZE, EZEE, EZZE, EEEE, EZZZ, and ZEZZ), which were uncharacterized until now. Our AIMS/BOMD simulation showed the natural evolution of the wavepacket across multiple ground-state species upon relaxing through the CI on the picosecond timescale. Additionally, we showed the key structural parameters involved in each step of DASA’s main multistep photoswitching mechanism, providing new insights to better control the open to close photoswitching mechanism (green in Figure 2). Overall, our ground- and excited-state dynamics suggest that the intramolecular hydrogen bond represents a key design parameter for inducing not only the Z/E photoisomerization in the actinic step, but also the 4p-electrocyclization on the ground-state, resulting in improved open-to-close performance. Also, we show a rich and diverse ground-state chemistry involving a complex interplay of interlinking reactions involving rotations about different carbon-carbon bonds along the hexatriene bridge that can compete with the productive photoswitching pathway. This study lays the foundation for a full kinetic and thermodynamic characterization of DASAs multi-timescale chemistry, which is fundamental in tuning and designing future DASA generations. Indeed, our simulations provide unprecedented details of the complete photoswitching mechanism of DASAs and showcases the state-of-the-art tools in unravelling complex, multistep, photoinitiated ground-state chemistry.
